title: How do you describe the output scripts a wallet should watch?
dek: The keys are only part of a wallet backup. A descriptor records how to turn them into the outputs the wallet should look for.

blocks.text: You restore a wallet from its seed. The keys are there, but which outputs should the wallet search for? The same public key can appear in several kinds of script. The seed also does not record which derivation paths the old wallet used. A backup can preserve the keys and still leave these questions unanswered.

An output script descriptor supplies those missing instructions. It names the script to build, the keys to put in it, and any steps needed to derive them. Another wallet can read that description and reproduce the same outputs instead of having to guess how the first wallet used its keys.

figure.title: One key does not identify one script
figure.caption: These four output scripts use the same public key. BIP 384’s combo() example produces all of them; a more specific expression, such as wpkh(), chooses a particular form.

sections.heading: Choose the script, not just the key

blocks.text: Look at pkh(KEY) and wpkh(KEY). Both use the hash of a public key, but they put it into different scripts. The letters before the parentheses settle that choice. The key alone cannot tell a restored wallet which form the original wallet used.

The expression is a recipe for ordinary Bitcoin script. With pkh(), the key’s 20-byte hash fills a slot between fixed instructions. Change the key and that slot changes. Change the function and the surrounding script changes too. Descriptors describe outputs that Bitcoin already supports; they do not introduce a new spending rule.

blocks.title: What pkh() adds around the key
blocks.caption: The highlighted slot holds the key’s hash. The surrounding instructions come from the pkh() template.

blocks.text: Functions can fit inside one another. In sh(wpkh(KEY)), wpkh() first produces the SegWit script. sh() then makes an output that commits to that script’s hash. The inner script becomes the redeemScript needed when spending. The parentheses preserve this relationship instead of leaving it for the receiving wallet to infer.

blocks.summary: Which functions can go inside which?

blocks.text: BIP 381 covers the three main standard formats from before SegWit: pk(), pkh() and sh(). BIP 382 adds wpkh() and wsh(). sh() is only allowed at the top level; wpkh() and wsh() can appear at the top or inside sh(). Keys in wpkh(), and anywhere under wsh(), must be compressed. BIP 386 adds tr(), whose keys are x-only. A checksum cannot make an invalid nesting valid.

sections.heading: Read the key’s past and future

blocks.text: The brackets before a key describe its past. They contain a fingerprint of the key where derivation began, followed by the path from there. This origin information helps a signer holding that root find the right private key. It is information for the wallet; it adds no instructions to the output script.

The path after an extended key describes what to do next. In the example below, the wallet starts from the supplied xpub, follows /1/2, and then derives a child at the final /*. Keep those two paths separate when reading: the bracketed path explains how the supplied key was reached; the suffix continues from it.

blocks.title: Past steps, supplied key, next steps
blocks.caption: The origin records earlier derivation. The path and wildcard after the xpub tell the wallet which keys to derive next.

blocks.text: A final /* makes this a ranged descriptor. It stands for a sequence of output scripts, one for each child index, so the wallet can keep deriving fresh receiving outputs from the same description. BIP 382 lists its first three. The interactive example reproduces those scripts from the published xpub.

Try a different expression in the example. Notice whether the output changes, whether the descriptor contains a private key, and whether it describes one script or several. The short strings in the drawing are abbreviations; the full descriptor and resulting scripts are available underneath.

blocks.title: From a description to its output scripts
blocks.caption: Choose a published example. Inspect its keys, resulting scripts and checksum; each expansion is checked against the scripts listed in the BIPs.

blocks.text: A key expression can contain a hex public key, a WIF private key, or an extended key. Hardened steps may be written with h or an apostrophe. BIP 381 publishes pkh() examples using both spellings, and using either a WIF private key or its corresponding public key. All produce the same output script. The origin records how to find a key, rather than changing what that key pays to.

sections.heading: What does sharing the line reveal?

blocks.text: A descriptor containing only public keys lets another wallet derive the scripts to watch without handing it the private keys needed to sign. That is useful for a watch-only export. It also reveals which outputs belong together. Public-key material can still carry information you would not want to publish.

A descriptor can also contain an xprv or a WIF private key. Those keys remain spending secrets when wrapped in a descriptor. Two lines that produce the same script may therefore have very different consequences if shared: one may expose a public key, while the other exposes its private counterpart.

Exporting a public descriptor sometimes requires more than replacing xprv with xpub. A public extended key cannot perform the intervening hardened derivations. The exporter has to move past those steps first, then record how it got there so a signer can still identify the key.

blocks.summary: The rule for removing private keys from an export

blocks.text: BIP 380 says the exporter should derive the extended public key at the last hardened derivation step and use that key in the descriptor. The steps taken to reach it must be added to the previous origin information. The remaining derivation then starts from the exported key.

A descriptor can end with # followed by an eight-character checksum. It gives the receiving software a way to notice that the text changed during copying. BIP 380 allows parsing without a checksum, but an application may require one. A # with nothing after it is a different case: the checksum is missing, and the test vector is rejected.

In the example, changing deadbeef to deedbeef while keeping the old checksum makes the check fail. But someone who deliberately changes the text can also calculate its new checksum. No secret key is involved. A matching checksum therefore cannot establish who supplied the descriptor or whether you should trust it.

blocks.title: A copying error and a deliberate edit
blocks.caption: The middle line keeps the old checksum and fails. The bottom line has a newly calculated checksum and passes, even though its payload is still changed.

blocks.summary: How the checksum works, and what it guarantees

blocks.text: The checksum uses a fixed set of 95, which BIP 380 describes as three groups of 32 (the last group is one short). Each character becomes its position in a group. After every third character, another symbol records the group numbers. This arrangement helps the checksum detect changes to the text.

Any single symbol error is always detected; any two or three in a descriptor up to 49,154 characters; any four up to 507; any five up to 77. Random errors go undetected with a chance of 1 in 2^40. The model reproduces BIP 380’s raw(deadbeef)#89f8spxm vector and checks all of its published checksum cases.

Those cases include a checksum that is too long or too short, an error in the payload, an error in the checksum, and an unsupported character. Checking the checksum and checking whether the descriptor is a valid expression are separate jobs.

For multisignature outputs, multi() records the threshold and the participating keys. sortedmulti() sorts the derived public keys before building the script. If the keys have ranges, they advance together using the same child index. That keeps the description of the joint output in one expression.

Other functions cover other needs. combo() expands one key into the older script forms shown at the top of this page. raw() carries an existing script directly, and addr() describes the script for an existing address. tr() describes a Taproot output, optionally including its tree of spending scripts.

blocks.title: A reference for placing expressions
blocks.caption: A dot marks an allowed context. Hatched rows belong to proposals outside this chapter’s source set.

blocks.summary: Multisig limits and the Taproot model’s scope

blocks.text: For multi(k, KEY_1, …, KEY_n), k must not exceed n. The context limits the key count: 3 at the top level, 15 compressed keys (or 7 uncompressed) directly inside sh() because of the 520-byte push limit, and 20 otherwise. sortedmulti() sorts keys lexicographically after derivation.

tr(KEY) produces an output with no usable script path; tr(KEY, TREE) adds a tree written with braces. Of the script expressions that existed when BIP 386 was written, only pk() could be a leaf. Miniscript and multi_a() came later. This site’s model supports pk() leaves and rejects the published Miniscript example as outside its scope.

These proposals were assigned in 2021 as BIPs 380 to 386 and are recorded as Deployed in the pinned sources. The BIPs record descriptors in Bitcoin Core since version 0.17, and tr() since 22.0. BIP 380’s index also lists later expressions such as musig() and sp().

The authors wanted descriptors to be readable by engineers familiar with Bitcoin’s existing formats. They also argued against encoding script choices in alternative extended-key version bytes: key derivation and script type are separate decisions. Descriptors give each an explicit place in the text.
